24	- "Make a chord sheet for <song>" starting from **lyrics only**, or from a
25	  **YouTube / Bilibili / SoundCloud link** or an **mp3 / wav** file.
26	- Ask about **lyrics sources** (Mojim/魔鏡, KKBOX, Musixmatch, LRCLIB, Genius,
27	  NetEase, QQ Music) — which give time-synced `.lrc` vs plain text.
28	
29	## When NOT to use
30	
31	- **Engraving staff notation** (notes on a staff, MusicXML / MIDI / LilyPond /
32	  MuseScore output) — ChordPro is lyrics+chords, not a score. Hand off to a
33	  notation tool. (ChordPro *can* embed ABC/LilyPond fragments — see the format
34	  reference — but it is not an engraver.)
35	- **OMR from a scanned score image** (photo/PDF of printed sheet music → notes)
36	  is out of scope; there is no reliable open path. Offer manual transcription
37	  into ChordPro instead, and say so plainly.
38	
39	## Authoritative sources
40	
41	- Format + directives + CLI: **https://www.chordpro.org/** (link, don't
42	  paraphrase from memory — the directive set evolves).
43	- Source / releases: **https://github.com/ChordPro/chordpro**.
44	
45	## The router — pick the workflow by what the user has
46	
47	| User has… | Do this | Reliability |
48	|---|---|---|
49	| A `.cho`/`.crd`/`.pro` file | Render / transpose / **validate** via `chordpro` CLI | High |
50	| **Chords-over-lyrics** text (UG/OnSong) | `a2crd` → light manual cleanup → validate | High |
51	| A **known song** (title / lyrics / a link) and no chords yet | **Search existing chord charts online** → adapt to ChordPro (often via `a2crd`) → validate. See `references/chord-tab-sources.md` | Med–High (**best first move**) |
52	| **Lyrics only**, no chart found | Fetch/confirm lyrics → **interactively** fill chords (propose from key, ask the user to confirm/correct) | Medium (human-in-loop) |
53	| An **audio file or link**, want a machine draft | `scripts/audio-to-chords.py` → *draft* with `AUTO-GENERATED` header → human correction | ~80% (last resort) |
54	
55	Prefer the highest row that fits. Two rules that matter: don't jump to the audio
56	pipeline when the user already pasted chords (`a2crd` is faster and correct); and
57	for a **named/popular song, search for an existing human-made chart first** — it's
58	usually more accurate than audio ACR and sidesteps the download-ToS problem
59	entirely.
60	
61	**Before charting a named song, confirm it exists as described** — user-supplied
62	artist/album is sometimes wrong, and searching a bad artist can grab a mislabeled
63	chart; a quick Wikipedia/LRCLIB match prevents shipping a misattribution.
64	**Non-interactive/batch runs** can't use the "ask the user" rows — instead produce a
65	best-effort chart from the published chord vocabulary, caption every uncertainty in
66	a `{comment:}`, and omit unknown metadata rather than fabricate it.
67	
68	## ChordPro cheat-sheet + output template
69	
70	- **Extensions**: `.cho` (recommended), also `.crd` `.chopro` `.chord` `.pro`.
71	  Plain UTF-8. `#` starts a comment line; blank lines separate blocks.
72	- **Inline chords**: `[C]` immediately before the syllable it sits over —
73	  `Swing [G]low, sweet [C]chari[G]ot`. Annotations (non-chords): `[*softly]`.
74	- **Metadata**: `{title:}`/`{t:}`, `{subtitle:}`/`{st:}`, `{artist:}`,
75	  `{composer:}`, `{album:}`, `{year:}`, `{key:}`, `{tempo:}`, `{time:}`, `{capo:}`.
76	- **Environments** (long / short): chorus `{start_of_chorus}`/`{soc}` …
77	  `{end_of_chorus}`/`{eoc}`; verse `{sov}`…`{eov}`; bridge `{sob}`…`{eob}`;
78	  tab (monospaced, chords NOT parsed) `{sot}`…`{eot}`. Recall a chorus with
79	  `{chorus}`. Comments: `{comment:}`/`{c:}`.
80	- **Key vs capo**: `{key:}` is the *written/fingering* key of the shapes shown;
81	  `{capo:}` is the capo used. If charts disagree, prefer the one whose chord
82	  vocabulary is internally consistent, and caption the *sounding* pitch.
83	- **Chorus recall**: `{chorus}` reprints the most-recently-defined chorus (showing
84	  only a "Chorus" label by default). With 2+ distinct recurring sections, label
85	  them — `{start_of_chorus: name}` … `{chorus: name}` — or expand the repeat.
86	
87	Emit this shape — metadata block → environments/comments → verses/choruses:
88	
89	```
90	{title: Swing Low Sweet Chariot}
91	{artist: Traditional}
92	{key: G}
93	{tempo: 90}
94	{time: 4/4}
95	
96	{comment: Intro}
97	[G] [C] [G] [D]
98	
99	{start_of_chorus: Chorus}
100	Swing [G]low, sweet [C]chari[G]ot,
101	Comin' for to carry me [D]home.
102	{end_of_chorus}
103	
104	{start_of_verse: Verse 1}
105	I [G]looked over Jordan, and [C]what did I [G]see,
106	Comin' for to carry me [D]home.
107	{end_of_verse}
108	
109	{chorus}
110	```
111	
112	Full directive set (chord `{define}` diagrams, `{transpose}`, markup, ABC/LilyPond
113	blocks, `x_` custom namespace) → read `references/chordpro-format.md`.
114	
115	## The `chordpro` / `a2crd` CLI (essentials)
116	
117	The official tool is a Perl program (CPAN dist **`App::Music::ChordPro`**). Current
118	6.x releases install the **`chordpro`** command; the chords-over-lyrics importer
119	is `chordpro --a2crd` (a standalone `a2crd` binary shipped in older releases and
120	may be absent — prefer `chordpro --a2crd`).
121	
122	```bash
123	# Install (macOS — there is NO official Homebrew formula; use CPAN)
124	brew install perl cpanminus && cpanm App::Music::ChordPro
125	# If `chordpro` then errors "Can't locate ChordPro.pm", activate local::lib once:
126	eval "$(perl -I"$HOME/perl5/lib/perl5" -Mlocal::lib)"   # add to ~/.zshrc to persist
127	
128	# Render
129	chordpro -o song.pdf song.cho          # PDF (format inferred from extension)
130	chordpro --generate=HTML -o song.html song.cho
131	
132	# Transpose (N semitones; suffix s/f forces sharp/flat spelling)
133	chordpro -x 2  -o up.pdf   song.cho
134	chordpro -x -3f -o down.pdf song.cho
135	
136	# Convert chords-over-lyrics text -> ChordPro (the official importer)
137	chordpro --a2crd input.txt -o song.cho
138	```
139	
140	Install-per-platform, generators, config JSON, songbook `--toc`, and `a2crd`
141	heuristic tuning → read `references/cli-and-rendering.md`.
142	
143	## Verify loop — never hand back an unvalidated `.cho`
144	
145	Every generated or edited file goes through the parser before you present it:
146	
147	```bash
148	scripts/validate-cho.sh song.cho          # wraps the command below; PASS/FAIL + warnings
149	# equivalently:
150	chordpro --strict --generate=Text -o - song.cho   # exit 0 + no stderr warnings = valid
151	```
152	
153	To auto-normalize to canonical form (fix spacing, round-trip directives):
154	`chordpro --generate=ChordPro -o song.cho song.cho`. If `chordpro` isn't
155	installed, the script prints the install one-liner — say so and offer to proceed
156	without rendering (the format is still human-checkable).
157	
158	**Producing a PDF? Verify it *renders*, not just parses.** `validate-cho.sh` only
159	checks that the file parses — it can't see a broken PDF. `chordpro`'s default
160	fonts have **no CJK glyphs**, so a Chinese/Japanese/Korean song renders as blank
161	tofu while still exiting 0 and passing validation. Use `scripts/render-cho.sh
162	song.cho` — it auto-detects a CJK font, renders, and glyph-checks the PDF (fails
163	loudly on tofu).
164	
165	## Finding existing chord charts (the usual first move)
166	
167	For a named/popular song, a human-made chart almost always already exists online
168	and beats audio extraction on accuracy. The realistic recipe (WebFetch's
169	summarizer strips copyrighted lyrics, and `a2crd`'s column logic mis-aligns
170	full-width CJK — so neither is the happy path it looks like):
171	
172	```bash
173	# 1. search (中文: 吉他谱/和弦/弹唱谱; EN: chords / ultimate guitar)
174	# 2. fetch the RAW html (WebFetch drops the lyrics) and parse chords from the
175	#    site's markup — e.g. Chord4 parenthesized-syllable, UG js-store data-content.
176	curl -sL "<chart-url>" -o chart.html
177	# 3. lyrics come SEPARATELY from LRCLIB (reliable, synced):
178	uv run scripts/fetch-lyrics.py --artist "…" --track "…" -o song.lrc
179	# 4. align the chart's chords onto the lyric syllables by phrase, NOT by column
180	#    (CJK chars are 2 display cells). For pure-Latin chords-over-lyrics you can
181	#    still use:  chordpro --a2crd chart.txt -o song.cho
182	scripts/validate-cho.sh song.cho && scripts/render-cho.sh song.cho   # 5. validate + render (CJK-safe)
183	```
184	
185	Caption the result with a `{comment:}` naming the source and "published
186	arrangement — verify against the recording (capo/key may differ)". Not machine
187	ACR, so no `AUTO-GENERATED` header. Per-site extraction patterns, the site catalog
188	(91譜/Chord4/UG — many are JS-rendered or image-only 六线谱), simplified↔traditional
189	handling, and legality → read `references/chord-tab-sources.md`.
190	
191	## Generating from audio / links — the fallback when no chart exists
192	
193	This is the shakiest path — reach for it only when no existing chart is available.
194	
195	**Set expectations first**: open automatic chord recognition tops out around **78–80% on simple major/minor pop**
196	and drops sharply on 7ths, extended/jazz chords, key changes, and quiet or dense
197	mixes; inversions/slash chords are unreliable; and it cannot know the capo a
198	guitarist used. Treat the result as a **draft to correct**, not a transcription.
199	
200	```bash
201	# Best-effort turnkey: link or local file -> draft ChordPro
202	uv run scripts/audio-to-chords.py --dry-run "https://youtu.be/..."   # show the plan first
203	uv run scripts/audio-to-chords.py -o draft.cho "https://youtu.be/..."
204	```
205	
206	The script downloads audio with `yt-dlp` (YouTube/Bilibili/SoundCloud) and runs
207	`chord-extractor`/Chordino. Its output **must** carry the
208	`{comment: AUTO-GENERATED — verify chords/key/timing}` header. On macOS the
209	Chordino Vamp plugin often isn't installed; the script detects that and prints
210	exact install guidance + manual alternatives instead of crashing — relay that to
211	the user rather than silently failing. Tool comparison, beat/key detection, and
212	commercial escape hatches (Moises/Songsterr have APIs; Chordify/Chord AI/Ultimate
213	Guitar don't) → read `references/audio-to-chords.md`.
214	
215	**Legal**: only process content the user owns or has the right to use, for
216	personal use, locally; downloading copyrighted audio can violate a platform's
217	ToS. Surface this — don't bury it.
218	
219	## Lyrics sources
220	
221	Default to **LRCLIB** — free, no API key, returns time-synced `.lrc`:
222	
223	```bash
224	uv run scripts/fetch-lyrics.py --artist "Adele" --track "Hello" --duration 295
225	uv run scripts/fetch-lyrics.py --plain --artist "..." --track "..."   # plain text
226	```
227	
228	| Source | Access | Synced `.lrc`? |
229	|---|---|---|
230	| **LRCLIB** | free, no key | **yes** |
231	| Musixmatch | API key; full/synced is paid | yes (paid) |
232	| NetEase / QQ Music | unofficial community APIs | yes (Chinese catalog) |
233	| Genius (`lyricsgenius`) | API token; lyrics scraped from page | no (plain) |
234	| Mojim / 魔鏡 | scrape-only | no (plain) |
235	| KKBOX | partner-gated | n/a |
236	
237	Full comparison, legality, and the LRCLIB API → read `references/lyrics-sources.md`.
238	
239	## Available scripts
240	
241	- **`scripts/validate-cho.sh <file.cho>`** — verify a file parses cleanly
242	  (`chordpro --strict`); PASS/FAIL to stdout, warnings to stderr. Guides install
243	  if `chordpro` is missing. Flags: `--help`.
244	- **`scripts/render-cho.sh <file.cho>`** — render to PDF with a **CJK-safe** font
245	  (auto-detected) and glyph-check the result, so a Chinese song can't silently
246	  render as tofu. Flags: `-o/--output`, `--font`, `--keep-config`, `--help`.
247	- **`scripts/fetch-lyrics.py`** — fetch lyrics from LRCLIB (synced `.lrc` default,
248	  `--plain` for text). Auto-retries a CJK miss with a romanized/pinyin query.
249	  Self-contained via `uv run`. Flags: `--artist`, `--track`, `--duration`,
250	  `--album`, `--plain`, `-o/--output`, `--help`, `--dry-run`.
251	- **`scripts/audio-to-chords.py`** — best-effort link/audio → draft ChordPro
252	  (`yt-dlp` + `chord-extractor`). Degrades gracefully when the ACR backend is
253	  unavailable. Flags: `-o/--output`, `--lrc`, `--help`, `--dry-run`.
254	
255	## Bundled assets
256	
257	Ready-to-open examples + a template under `assets/` (all songs are **public
258	domain**; every `.cho` validates clean with `chordpro --strict`). Use them as
259	copy-paste starting points and few-shot references:
260	
261	- `assets/example-amazing-grace.cho` — simplest real song: metadata + inline chords.
262	- `assets/example-when-the-saints.cho` — chorus/verse structure + `{chorus}` recall.
263	- `assets/example-greensleeves.cho` — feature showcase: `{define}` diagrams, a
264	  `{sot}` tab block, chorus recall, transpose note.
265	- `assets/template-song.cho` — fill-in-the-blanks scaffold (renders as-is); the
266	  starting point for the interactive chord-fill flow.
267	- `assets/example-synced-lyrics.lrc` — sample time-synced `.lrc` (what
268	  `fetch-lyrics.py` returns; feed it to `audio-to-chords.py --lrc`).
269	- `assets/example-a2crd-input.txt` — chords-over-lyrics plain text; convert with
270	  `chordpro --a2crd assets/example-a2crd-input.txt`.
271	
272	## Reference files
273	
274	- `references/chordpro-format.md` — Read **when** hand-authoring or you need a
275	  directive beyond the cheat-sheet (`{define}` diagrams, `{transpose}`, markup,
276	  ABC/LilyPond, `x_` custom namespace).
277	- `references/chord-tab-sources.md` — Read **when** you need chords for a named
278	  song and have none: where to find existing charts (91譜/Chord4/Ultimate
279	  Guitar/…), how to adapt them, and the legality.
280	- `references/cli-and-rendering.md` — Read **when** installing, rendering,
281	  transposing, converting with `a2crd`, or validating/normalizing.
282	- `references/audio-to-chords.md` — Read **when** the user wants chords from an
283	  audio file or a link (ACR tool choice, beat/key, limits, escape hatches).
284	- `references/lyrics-sources.md` — Read **when** fetching lyrics (source table,
285	  synced-vs-plain, API-vs-scrape, legality, LRCLIB API).
286	
287	## Gotchas
288	
289	- **macOS has no official Homebrew `chordpro`** — install via CPAN
290	  (`brew install perl cpanminus && cpanm App::Music::ChordPro`). A signed `.dmg`
291	  GUI exists on GitHub Releases but the CLI is the CPAN route.
292	- **`Can't locate ChordPro.pm in @INC` after cpanm** — cpanm installed into a
293	  `local::lib` (`~/perl5`) that isn't on Perl's path. Activate it:
294	  `eval "$(perl -I"$HOME/perl5/lib/perl5" -Mlocal::lib)"` (persist in `~/.zshrc`).
295	- **No standalone `a2crd` in ChordPro 6.x** — use `chordpro --a2crd input.txt`.
296	  Its output needs a human pass (heuristic, column-based chord placement); always
297	  validate and eyeball before rendering.
298	- **Angle brackets `< >` are text markup in ChordPro v6.** Don't put `<...>`
299	  placeholders in lyrics/chords — the parser reads `<b>`/`<i>`-style markup and
300	  floods warnings. Use plain-text placeholders (see `assets/template-song.cho`).
301	- **No official online validator.** chordpro.org hosts docs + a desktop GUI, not
302	  a "try it online" box. Validate locally with the CLI (`validate-cho.sh`).
303	- **CJK renders as tofu by default — and passes validation.** `chordpro`'s default
304	  fonts have no Han/Kana/Hangul glyphs, so a Chinese/Japanese/Korean song produces
305	  a blank PDF that still exits 0 and passes `validate-cho.sh` (which only checks
306	  parsing). Render CJK with `scripts/render-cho.sh` (auto CJK font + glyph-check),
307	  or pass `--config` pointing `pdf.fonts.*` at a CJK font.
308	- **`a2crd` is Latin-only.** Its column heuristic assumes 1 char = 1 column, but
309	  full-width CJK occupies 2 display cells, so chords drift. For CJK, align chords to
310	  syllables/phrases by musical judgment — don't trust column arithmetic.
311	- **A strict "Unknown chord" warning ≠ a parse error.** `chordpro --strict` warns
312	  "Unknown chord" for a *valid* chord it has no built-in diagram for (e.g. `Em/C#`,
313	  `F#m7b5`); it still renders. Add a `{define}` (see the format reference) or ignore.
314	- **`{chorus}` recall is a trap with 2+ recurring sections.** It reprints only the
315	  most-recently-defined chorus, as a bare "Chorus" tag by default. Label distinct
316	  blocks (`{start_of_chorus: name}` / `{chorus: name}`) or expand repeats explicitly.
317	- **`WebFetch` strips copyrighted lyrics** (returns "[lyrics omitted]"), so the
318	  chart-fetch path needs raw `curl` + per-site parsing; and from an image-only chart
319	  `WebFetch` may *fabricate* chord placement — trust only an explicit chord list.
320	- **Chord accuracy from audio is ~80% at best** on simple pop, worse otherwise.
321	  Never present a machine-extracted sheet without the `AUTO-GENERATED` header and
322	  a "verify chords/key/timing" caveat.
323	- **Auto-generated chart sites are ACR in disguise.** Chordu / Chordify /
324	  GuitarTuna charts are machine-derived (~80%, same caveat) — treat them as drafts,
325	  unlike human-made charts on 91譜 / Chord4 / Ultimate Guitar.
326	- **Detected key is a suggestion.** ACR outputs absolute pitches; key detection
327	  confuses relative major/minor and keys a fifth apart, and enharmonic spelling
328	  (Gb vs F#) is ambiguous. Confirm with the user before committing `{key:}`.
329	- **Chords in `{sot}`…`{eot}` tab blocks are NOT parsed** — that's for ASCII tab.
330	  Use inline `[..]` in verses/choruses; reserve tab blocks for fret diagrams.
331	- **Lyrics/audio ToS.** Prefer LRCLIB (open); most other lyric sources are
332	  scrape-only or paid, and downloading audio has copyright/ToS limits. Keep it
333	  personal-use and local; surface the caveat rather than hiding it.
334

<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleRoman.html`

```text
What romanNumeralFromChord does and how to call it
- roman.romanNumeralFromChord takes a music21 Chord and returns a music21.roman.RomanNumeral object.
- It is called like: roman.romanNumeralFromChord(chordObj, keyObj=None, preferSecondaryDominants=False)
- As the docs put it: "Takes a chord object and returns an appropriate chord name." (<=125 chars)

Notes about chord-symbol parsing
- The roman API works from Chord objects (music21.chord.Chord). Parsing text chord symbols such as "F#m7b5", "Cadd9", "G/B" is not done by roman. The docs point users to the harmony/ChordSymbol class for that task: note the reference to the "harmonic.ChordSymbol class for parsing chord symbols" (paraphrased from the doc). Use harmony.ChordSymbol to parse text into a Chord/ChordSymbol, then feed the resulting chord into romanNumeralFromChord if you want a Roman numeral.

How to get scale-degree, quality, and figure from the returned RomanNumeral
- The function returns a RomanNumeral instance (e.g. <music21.roman.RomanNumeral vio in c minor>).
- Important properties:
  - scaleDegree: the degree number (int). Example: roman.RomanNumeral('vi','E').scaleDegree -> 6
  - quality: chord quality (inherited from Chord). Example: rn.quality returns 'major' / 'minor' / 'diminished' / etc.
  - figure: the full figure string as parsed. Example: roman.RomanNumeral('bVII65/V','C').figure -> 'bVII65/V'
- You can also read romanNumeral.figureAndKey (e.g. 'V65/V in e minor') and romanNumeral.romanNumeral (the front-altered numeral like '#II' or 'Ger').

Example workflow (conceptual)
1. Parse text symbol -> harmony.ChordSymbol (or create chord.Chord).
2. Call roman.romanNumeralFromChord(chordObj, keyObj) to get a RomanNumeral.
3. Inspect rn.scaleDegree, rn.quality, rn.figure (and rn.figureAndKey / rn.romanNumeral) for the requested info.

Concise quote from doc
- "Takes a chord object and returns an appropriate chord name." (<=125 chars)
```

High-level, foundational algorithms and analyses
- The Krumhansl–Schmuckler (KS) pitch-class/profile correlation method is the classic, widely-used key‑finding approach: build a 12‑dim pitch-class distribution (chroma) and correlate it with major/minor key templates. # Chord4 (chord4.com / 和弦网)

### Access
Bare `curl` is Cloudflare-blocked (returns a 5,464-byte "Attention Required" page). It works with a browser `User-Agent` + `Accept-Language` header and `--compressed`. Real page is ~71 KB.

### Container — confirmed
The skill's note is CORRECT. Exactly one `<div class="tabs_content">` holding exactly one `<pre>...</pre>`. The ENTIRE chart — credits, key/capo, chord-fingering table, and the chords-over-lyrics body — is plain text inside that single `<pre>`. There are NO HTML tags inside the `<pre>`.

### Chord-to-syllable binding — the REAL mechanism (skill claim (a) is right, (b) is WRONG)

`data-chord` does NOT bind syllables. The 15 `data-chord="..."` attributes are on the chord-diagram gallery and sit AFTER `</pre>`:
```
<div class="chord-image-item" data-chord="Bb">
  <div class="chord-image-header"><span class="chord-label">Bb</span>
```
(Pre block ends at byte 10917; first `data-chord` is at byte 11497. They just enumerate the unique chords, one SVG diagram each.)

The actual binding is a TWO-LINE plain-text pattern with ordinal parenthesis-pairing:
- A CHORD line: chord tokens separated by spaces, with `|` bar separators.
- A LYRIC line directly below with inline markers `( )` (empty) or `(字)` (wrapping one syllable).
- Binding is ORDINAL: the Nth chord token pairs with the Nth `(...)` marker, left to right. `|` bars are NOT counted.

Verbatim (≤2 lyric lines):
```
| G                | F#m7       B7 
 ( ) 沒有了聯絡 後來的生(活) 我都是聽(別)人說
```
Chords in order `G, F#m7, B7` ↔ markers `( ), (活), (別)`. So F#m7 lands on 活, B7 on 別, and G is a lead-in with no syllable (empty `( )`). I verified the counts match across many lines (e.g. an 8-chord line `| G B7 | Em7 G/D | Cmaj7 D7 | G D7` ↔ exactly 8 markers).

Crucial consequence: alignment is NOT whitespace-column based. You do NOT need monospace/CJK-double-width column reconstruction. Just `re.findall(r'\(([^)]*)\)', lyricLine)` zipped in order against the chord tokens. Chord attaches immediately before the char inside its marker.

### Lines and sections
- Lines = literal newlines in the `<pre>`.
- Section/part labels = bracketed tokens on their own line: in this chart `[Piano]`, `[String]` (instrument/arrangement parts, in English — NOT 前奏/主歌/副歌 here). These use square brackets, i.e. the same delimiter as ChordPro chords, but in the SOURCE they are standalone lines, so distinguish "a whole line is `[Word]`" = label vs. chord lines which never use brackets.
- Repeats: `*` markers. `* (…)` opens a block, `… *` closes it, and a later `Repeat *` line re-invokes it.

### Instrumental bars / intro
Represented as a chord line followed by a lyric line containing ONLY `( )` (no CJK):
```
[Piano]
| G B7 | Em7 G/D | Cmaj7 D7 | G D7
( )
```
IMPORTANT ASYMMETRY: here there are 8 chords but a single `( )` marker — the 1:1 ordinal pairing deliberately breaks. Parser rule: if the lyric line has no word/CJK characters (only `( )` and spaces), treat the block as instrumental and emit all chords bare (with their `|` bars), rather than trying to pair.

### Metadata (all machine-parseable)
Inside the `<pre>`, as plain text at the top (regex-able directly):
```
詞: 方文山 …        (lyricist)
曲: 周杰倫 …        (composer)
編配者：EvsBe@…      (arranger)
------------------------------------
Key=Bb   Play=G    Capo=3

The ENTIRE chart — credits, key/capo, chord-fingering table, and the chords-over-lyrics body — is plain text inside that single `&lt;pre&gt;`. There are NO HTML tags inside the `&lt;pre&gt;`.

### Chord-to-syllable binding — the REAL mechanism (skill claim (a) is right, (b) is WRONG)

`data-chord` does NOT bind syllables. The 15 `data-chord="..."` attributes are on the chord-diagram gallery and sit AFTER `&lt;/pre&gt;`:
```
&lt;div class="chord-image-item" data-chord="Bb"&gt;
  &lt;div class="chord-image-header"&gt;&lt;span class="chord-label"&gt;Bb&lt;/span&gt;
```
(Pre block ends at byte 10917; first `data-chord` is at byte 11497. They just enumerate the unique chords, one SVG diagram each.)

The actual binding is a TWO-LINE plain-text pattern with ordinal parenthesis-pairing:
- A CHORD line: chord tokens separated by spaces, with `|` bar separators.
- A LYRIC line directly below with inline markers `( )` (empty) or `(字)` (wrapping one syllable).
- Binding is ORDINAL: the Nth chord token pairs with the Nth `(...)` marker, left to right. `|` bars are NOT counted.

Verbatim (≤2 lyric lines):
```
| G                | F#m7       B7 
 ( ) 沒有了聯絡 後來的生(活) 我都是聽(別)人說
```
Chords in order `G, F#m7, B7` ↔ markers `( ), (活), (別)`. So F#m7 lands on 活, B7 on 別, and G is a lead-in with no syllable (empty `( )`). I verified the counts match across many lines (e.g. an 8-chord line `| G B7 | Em7 G/D | Cmaj7 D7 | G D7` ↔ exactly 8 markers).

Crucial consequence: alignment is NOT whitespace-column based. You do NOT need monospace/CJK-double-width column reconstruction. Just `re.findall(r'\(([^)]*)\)', lyricLine)` zipped in order against the chord tokens. Chord attaches immediately before the char inside its marker.

### Lines and sections
- Lines = literal newlines in the `&lt;pre&gt;`.
- Section/part labels = bracketed tokens on their own line: in this chart `[Piano]`, `[String]` (instrument/arrangement parts, in English — NOT 前奏/主歌/副歌 here). These use square brackets, i.e. the same delimiter as ChordPro chords, but in the SOURCE they are standalone lines, so distinguish "a whole line is `[Word]`" = label vs. chord lines which never use brackets.
- Repeats: `*` markers. `* (…)` opens a block, `… *` closes it, and a later `Repeat *` line re-invokes it.

### Instrumental bars / intro
Represented as a chord line followed by a lyric line containing ONLY `( )` (no CJK):
```
[Piano]
| G B7 | Em7 G/D | Cmaj7 D7 | G D7
( )
```
IMPORTANT ASYMMETRY: here there are 8 chords but a single `( )` marker — the 1:1 ordinal pairing deliberately breaks. Parser rule: if the lyric line has no word/CJK characters (only `( )` and spaces), treat the block as instrumental and emit all chords bare (with their `|` bars), rather than trying to pair.

### Metadata (all machine-parseable)
Inside the `&lt;pre&gt;`, as plain text at the top (regex-able directly):

曲: 周杰倫 …        (composer)
編配者：EvsBe@…      (arranger)
------------------------------------
Key=Bb   Play=G    Capo=3
F#m7  202220        (chord-fingering table: name + frets, x = muted)
```
`Key=` written key, `Play=` sounding key with capo, `Capo=` fret. These appear ONLY inside the `&lt;pre&gt;` (grep found `Key=Bb`/`Play=G`/`Capo=3` exactly once each). Additionally, the page head has:

- `&lt;meta property="og:title" content="說好不哭 - 周杰倫 - 吉他譜 - Chord4"&gt;`, plus description/keywords.

### Simplified vs traditional
Server-side conversion, same numeric tab id:

# Research: music-theory validation helper for the ChordPro skill

Context grounding: the existing skill lives at `/Users/david/Documents/Program/agent-skills/skills/local/chordpro/`. Its two Python helpers (`scripts/fetch-lyrics.py`, `scripts/audio-to-chords.py`) are already self-contained `uv run` scripts, and `SKILL.md` already lists a relevant gotcha — *"Detected key is a suggestion… key detection confuses relative major/minor and keys a fifth apart, and enharmonic spelling (Gb vs F#) is ambiguous."* A key/plausibility validator slots naturally next to those as `scripts/analyze-key.py` (or similar) + a `references/music-theory.md` doc. Everything below is scoped to that.

## Bottom line (the recommended design)

- **Hand-roll the core, zero deps; offer `music21` only as an opt-in escalation.** For "parse chord symbol → root/quality/bass → Roman numeral / Nashville number in a given key," a ~150–250 line pure-Python module is tractable and *more* honest (you control the enharmonic spelling and the labels). `music21` is a pure-Python wheel but drags in **numpy + matplotlib** (plus chardet, jsonpickle, requests, joblib, webcolors) — heavyweight and slow-cold-start for a "lean" validator, and its `ChordSymbol` parser has documented edge-case bugs. Keep it as an optional PEP 723 extra for users who want its Krumhansl/Aarden key-finder or secondary-dominant detection.
- **Transition model: a small, hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral matrix, seeded from the de Clercq–Temperley Rock Corpus** (the one citable, CC BY 4.0, *pop/rock* transition source). Ship the tiny matrix inline; do **not** ship a dataset. Optionally allow a live Hooktheory Trends API escalation.
- **Key-fit: diatonic-membership count minus a circle-of-fifths distance penalty for non-diatonic chords, pick the best key, then disambiguate relative major/minor with first/last-chord + cadence weighting.**
- **Verdict = two independent axes:** per-chord *diatonic-fit* label (is the chord in the key?) and per-transition *plausibility* score (is the move common?). Combine, but keep them separate in the output — that's what makes it explainable and honest.

---

## 1. Roman-numeral analysis + key detection — library vs hand-roll

### What `music21` actually gives you

- **Roman numerals:** `roman.romanNumeralFromChord(chordObj, keyObj=None, preferSecondaryDominants=False)` returns a `RomanNumeral` with `.scaleDegree` (int), `.quality`, `.figure` (e.g. `'bVII65/V'`), `.figureAndKey`, `.romanNumeral`. It even does secondary-dominant labelling. Docs: [music21.roman module](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleRoman.html), [User's Guide ch. 23](https://music21.org/music21docs/usersGuide/usersGuide_23_romanNumerals.html).
- **Chord-symbol parsing is a *different* class:** `roman` works on `chord.Chord` objects, not text. Text symbols like `"F#m7b5"`, `"Cadd9"`, `"G/B"` go through `harmony.ChordSymbol(...)` → returns a Chord you then feed to `romanNumeralFromChord`. Docs: [music21.harmony](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleHarmony.html).
- **Key detection:** `stream.analyze('key')` delegates to `analysis.discrete`, which ships multiple profile weightings — Krumhansl–Schmuckler / Krumhansl–Kessler, Aarden-Essen, Bellman–Budge, Temperley–Kostka–Payne, Simple. Docs: [analysis.discrete](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleAnalysisDiscrete.html), [User's Guide ch. 15](https://music21.org/music21docs/usersGuide/usersGuide_15_key.html). (Confirm exact class names against `analysis.discrete` at build time — the search surfaced Krumhansl and Aarden-Essen in core but the naming is worth a one-line check.)

### Dependency weight / `uv run` behavior

- The `music21` wheel itself is **`py3-none-any` (pure Python)**, Python **>=3.10**, but its **runtime deps are numpy, matplotlib, chardet, jsonpickle, requests, more-itertools, webcolors, joblib** ([piwheels metadata](https://www.piwheels.org/project/music21/), [pyproject.toml](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/blob/master/pyproject.toml), [requirements.txt](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/blob/master/requirements.txt)). numpy and matplotlib carry **compiled binary wheels** — they resolve fine under `uv run` on mainstream macOS/Linux/Windows (prebuilt wheels exist), but they're the opposite of "lean": tens of MB, non-trivial cold resolve, and matplotlib is pure dead weight for a text validator. `uv` will cache it, so it's a one-time cost, but it still bloats the script's dependency surface.

### `ChordSymbol` parsing gotchas (the reason not to lean on it)

Known open bugs bite exactly the chords a ChordPro sheet contains: [#1570 — `addb7` yields a doubly-flatted seventh; slash chords with extensions decode wrong](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/issues/1570), and [#197 — invalid behavior with `sus`/`aug`](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/issues/197). `m7b5` (half-diminished) and basic `add9` are supported via `CHORD_TYPES`, and you can extend that dict, but you'd be normalizing strings *before* handing them over anyway — at which point you've already written most of a parser.

### The hand-roll — tractable, and the fiddly parts

Very tractable for this narrow job. The pieces:

1. **Chord-symbol tokenizer** (~40–70 lines): regex `root (A–G, #/b) | quality suffix | /bass`. Root+bass → pitch-class 0–11. Quality → a small set (maj, min, dim, aug, dom7, maj7, min7, m7b5, sus2/4, add9, 6…). You only need *quality* to a resolution that affects the Roman-numeral case (upper vs lower) and any °/ø/+ decoration.
2. **Diatonic-triad tables** (two 7-row tables):
   - Major: **I ii iii IV V vi vii°** (maj, min, min, maj, maj, min, dim).
   - Minor: **i ii° III iv v/V VI VII/vii°** — natural minor is `i ii° III iv v VI VII`; harmonic-minor practice raises 7 so `v→V` and `VII→vii°`. Handle both variants.
3. **Roman/Nashville emitter**: degree number relative to the key's tonic, cased by quality, prefixed with accidental for non-diatonic roots (`bVII`, `#iv`), figured-bass suffix for inversions from the `/bass` (`6`, `6/4`).

The genuinely fiddly bits — flag these in the reference doc:

- **Enharmonic spelling is not `pc % 12`.** You must spell each root by *letter name relative to the key's scale*, or you'll mislabel `bVII` vs `#VI`, or call IV in F-major (`Bb`) a `#III`. Build a per-key letter-spelled scale (key-signature aware), then compute the degree by letter distance, and derive the accidental from the actual vs. diatonic pitch. This is the single most error-prone part and the main thing `music21` gets right for free.
- **Minor-key harmonic/natural variants:** decide whether to report `v` or `V`, `bVII` or `vii°`, and whether a raised-6/7 chord is diatonic-in-context. Simplest honest rule: treat *both* natural and harmonic/melodic diatonic sets as "in key," and label the mode variant.
- **Borrowed / secondary chords:** you can cheaply label a fixed common set — mixture chords `bVII bIII bVI iv`, Neapolitan `bII`, and secondary dominants (a major/dom7 chord whose root is a fifth above a diatonic degree → `V/x`). Full, reliable secondary-dominant/augmented-sixth analysis is where you'd escalate to `music21`.
- **Slash chords:** map `/bass` to inversion figured bass when the bass is a chord tone, else note it as a pedal/added bass (`IV/1` style) rather than forcing a wrong inversion.

### Recommendation for section 1

**Hand-roll the core (zero deps), escalate to `music21` optionally.** The parse-and-label job is small, and hand-rolling keeps the output *explainable* (you emit the exact Roman/Nashville strings the user thinks in) and dodges the `ChordSymbol` bugs. Reserve `music21` — behind a PEP 723 `[project.optional-dependencies]`/`--with` flag or a `try: import` — for two things it does markedly better: **profile-based key detection** (Krumhansl/Aarden) as a cross-check, and **secondary-dominant / chromatic analysis** when the hand-roll labels something "out-of-key" that's really a `V/V`.

## 2. Chord-transition probability model

### Citable empirical sources (what's actually usable)

| Source | What it is | Usable how | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| **de Clercq & Temperley, "A Corpus Analysis of Rock Harmony," *Popular Music* 30/1 (2011)** + **Rock Corpus** ([paper PDF](https://davidtemperley.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/declercq-temperley-pm11.pdf), [rockcorpus.midside.com](https://rockcorpus.midside.com/)) | RS 5×20 (~99 songs) / RS 200 (200 songs), dual expert Roman-numeral harmonic analyses + timing/melody in v2.x; ships the extraction scripts | **The single best fit.** Small, *pop/rock*, Roman-numeral-native. Aggregate a first-order matrix from the analyses, or just hand-transcribe the headline transition tendencies into a tiny inline matrix. | **CC BY 4.0** — you can ship derived numbers with attribution |
| **McGill Billboard** ([DDMAL](https://ddmal.ca/research/The_McGill_Billboard_Project_%28Chord_Analysis_Dataset%29/)) + **corpusmusic/bb-cluster** ([repo](https://github.com/corpusmusic/bb-cluster)) | Billboard Hot 100 sample, expert chord annotations; the repo has `chord_by_chord.csv`, `songbysongtransprob.csv`, and `transitionprob.py` (per-song transition probabilities already computed) | Bigger, but absolute-chord not Roman-numeral by default (`parse.py` adds key-relative function). Good for a richer offline matrix if you want one. | Dataset varies; **bb-cluster code is GPL-3.0** (a copyleft caveat if you vendor it) |
| **Hooktheory Trends API** ([docs](https://www.hooktheory.com/api/trends/docs)) | `GET /v1/trends/nodes?cp=…` returns, for a scale-degree progression, the array of next chords with `probability` — literally an empirical next-chord oracle over the TheoryTab DB | **Live escalation** only: needs a free-account bearer token (`POST /v1/users/auth` → `activkey`), 10 req/10 s. Network + auth dependency, not shippable offline. | Proprietary; API-gated |
| **CoCoPops / Billboard** ([repo](https://github.com/Computational-Cognitive-Musicology-Lab/CoCoPops)) | Humdrum re-encoding of McGill Billboard | Alt encoding if you prefer Humdrum tooling | — |
| **Chordonomicon** ([arXiv 2410.22046](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.22046)) | 666k songs' chord progressions | Overkill to ship; cite as "big-data corroboration" | — |
| **UMass "Fundamentals of Music Theory," Unit 18** ([page](https://fundamentalsofmusictheory.umasscreate.net/unit-18/)) | Reproduces a pop/rock two-chord succession table (from the rock corpus) side-by-side with a classical one | Handy secondary citation; source of the concrete `V→IV = 28%` (pop) vs `7%` (classical) datapoint | — |

**Key empirical facts to bake into the prior and the caveats** (from de Clercq–Temperley / UMass): rock is **less goal-directed** than classical; **IV** is the most common non-tonic and **plagal IV→I** is pervasive; **`bVII→IV→I`** ("double-plagal") is a signature rock move; **`V→IV`** (a classical "retrogression") happens ~**28%** of the time in pop vs ~**7%** classical. The load-bearing consequence: **a classical-syntax transition prior will over-flag legitimate rock progressions.** Use a rock-derived prior, and say so.

### The functional-harmony theory prior (the defensible hand-authored option)

Yes — a small hand-authored first-order matrix over Roman-numeral *functions* is a standard, defensible approach for *validation* (as opposed to generation). Map degrees to functions — **T** = I, vi, (iii); **PD/S** = IV, ii; **D** = V, vii° — and encode the canonical tendencies: **V→I strong, ii→V→I, IV→I (plagal), IV→V, vi→IV, V→vi (deceptive), I→anything**, with low weight on true retrogressions (but *not* zero, per the rock data). References for the function mapping and tendencies: [Open Music Theory — Harmonic Functions](https://openmusictheory.github.io/harmonicFunctions.html), [Wikipedia — I–V–vi–IV progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I%E2%80%93V%E2%80%93vi%E2%80%93IV_progression). Markov-over-chords is a well-trodden method (e.g. the ["Write Like Taylor Swift" first-order chord Markov chain](https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/113839_da12af8738fb4774a22bd62f35666287.html)).

### Recommendation for section 2

Ship a **hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral transition matrix (~7×7 diatonic + a few common chromatic rows like `bVII`, `V/V`), with the numbers anchored to the de Clercq–Temperley rock corpus**, not to classical theory. This is the simplest *defensible, citable, offline* model. Score a progression as the mean (or geometric mean) log-probability of its steps; flag any step below a percentile/threshold as "suspect." Offer the **Hooktheory `/trends/nodes` API as an optional live cross-check** for users who want empirical current-DB probabilities.

**Combining the two axes into a readable verdict** — keep them orthogonal:

- **Diatonic-fit** flags the *chord* (in-key / borrowed / secondary / out-of-key).
- **Transition-probability** flags the *move* (this step is rare).
- A chord can be diatonic yet a rare move, or non-diatonic yet an extremely common move (`bVII`, `V/V`). So the strongest "**likely mis-transcribed**" signal is **the conjunction**: a low-probability transition *into* a chord that's also out-of-key. A rare move into a diatonic chord is "unusual but plausible"; a borrowed chord reached by a common move is "colorful, fine." Present per-chord labels and per-transition scores separately, then a combined verdict.

---

## 3. Circle of fifths for key-fit / detection

**Scoring recipe (simple, explainable):** for each of the 24 candidate keys, `score(K) = (# chords diatonic in K) − λ · Σ(circle-of-fifths distance of each non-diatonic chord root from K's tonic)`. Pick the argmax. Circle-of-fifths distance encodes relatedness: a chord one step around the circle (e.g. the V's own dominant, or `bVII`) is "near" and cheap; a tritone away is "far" and expensive. This is a lightweight, deterministic stand-in for the Krumhansl–Schmuckler profile correlation, and it's fully auditable (you can print the per-key tally). Background: [rnhart.net — key-finding / Krumhansl–Schmuckler](https://rnhart.net/articles/key-finding/), [Temperley 1999 KS re-evaluation](https://davidtemperley.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/temperley-mp99.pdf), [interactive circle of fifths + diatonic sets](https://www.guitarcomposerstoolbox.com/circle-of-fifths/). If you want a probabilistically-grounded variant, weight chord roots by a key profile instead of a flat diatonic count — that's exactly what `music21`'s Krumhansl/Aarden classes do, and is the natural escalation.

**The relative-major/minor pitfall (C vs Am):** they share an identical diatonic set, so *diatonic membership alone cannot tell them apart* — this is the canonical key-detection failure, which [MIREX Audio Key Detection](https://www.music-ir.org/mirex/wiki/2026%3AAudio_Key_Detection) even codifies by giving *partial credit* for relative/parallel/fifth errors. Disambiguate with **tonic-emphasis cues, not the pitch-class set**:

- **First and (especially) last chord** — progressions tend to start and end on the tonic. The final chord is the strongest single cue.
- **Cadence weighting** — a `V→I` at a phrase end nails major; `V→i` (or `bVII→i`, `iv→i`) nails minor. (This is precisely the fix the practitioner literature recommends for tools that mis-call minor: [goatwaveaudio — fixing AI key detection](https://goatwaveaudio.com/blog/fixing-ai-key-detection/).)
- **Bass / duration emphasis** — total time or count the presumed tonic chord dominates.
- If it's genuinely ambiguous, **report both and say so** (honest > confident-wrong), consistent with the skill's existing "Detected key is a suggestion" gotcha.

---

## Concrete recommended design (put this in `references/music-theory.md`)

**Dependency choice:** zero-dep hand-rolled core in a PEP 723 `uv run` script; `music21` behind an optional extra / `try-import` for (a) Krumhansl/Aarden key cross-check and (b) secondary-dominant analysis. Matches the skill's existing self-contained-script convention.

**Pipeline:** ChordPro `[..]` extraction → chord-symbol parse (root+quality+bass) → candidate-key scoring (diatonic count − λ·circle-distance) → relative-major/minor disambiguation (first/last chord + cadence) → Roman-numeral + Nashville emission in the chosen key → per-chord diatonic-fit labels → first-order transition scoring against the rock-corpus-seeded matrix → verdict.

**Transition model:** inline hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral matrix, numbers anchored to de Clercq–Temperley (CC BY 4.0, attribute it); optional Hooktheory `/trends/nodes` live cross-check.

**Output verdict — what it should look like:**

- **Detected key** + confidence, with the runner-up named when relative/parallel is close ("G major, or possibly E minor — final chord is G, so G major").
- **Per-chord table:** `chord | Roman | Nashville | label` where label ∈ {diatonic, borrowed (bVII…), secondary (V/V…), out-of-key}.
- **Per-transition flags:** the low-probability steps, each shown as `Xrare→ Y (p≈…, expected: …)`, framed as **"review — surprising but maybe intentional,"** *not* "wrong."
- **Overall plausibility score** (0–1 or a letter), = combination of diatonic-fit ratio and mean transition log-prob.
- **Suspect list** = the conjunction cases (out-of-key chord reached by a rare move) → *"likely mis-transcribed; double-check."*
- **Honesty footer:** the prior is rock-derived and descriptive, not prescriptive; unusual ≠ wrong; key may be ambiguous.

**Honest caveats to surface in the doc:** (1) a first-order Markov prior can't see the actual voice-leading or a modulation, so it flags surprising-but-valid moves — hence "review," not "error"; (2) rock legitimately breaks classical rules (`V→IV`, `bVII→IV→I`), so a classical prior over-flags — use the rock prior; (3) relative-major/minor is fundamentally ambiguous from the chord set alone; (4) enharmonic spelling depends on the chosen key, so a wrong key detection cascades into wrong Roman numerals.

# Research: music-theory validation helper for the ChordPro skill

Context grounding: the existing skill lives at `/Users/david/Documents/Program/agent-skills/skills/local/chordpro/`. Its two Python helpers (`scripts/fetch-lyrics.py`, `scripts/audio-to-chords.py`) are already self-contained `uv run` scripts, and `SKILL.md` already lists a relevant gotcha — *"Detected key is a suggestion… key detection confuses relative major/minor and keys a fifth apart, and enharmonic spelling (Gb vs F#) is ambiguous."* A key/plausibility validator slots naturally next to those as `scripts/analyze-key.py` (or similar) + a `references/music-theory.md` doc. Everything below is scoped to that.

## Bottom line (the recommended design)

- **Hand-roll the core, zero deps; offer `music21` only as an opt-in escalation.** For "parse chord symbol → root/quality/bass → Roman numeral / Nashville number in a given key," a ~150–250 line pure-Python module is tractable and *more* honest (you control the enharmonic spelling and the labels). `music21` is a pure-Python wheel but drags in **numpy + matplotlib** (plus chardet, jsonpickle, requests, joblib, webcolors) — heavyweight and slow-cold-start for a "lean" validator, and its `ChordSymbol` parser has documented edge-case bugs. Keep it as an optional PEP 723 extra for users who want its Krumhansl/Aarden key-finder or secondary-dominant detection.
- **Transition model: a small, hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral matrix, seeded from the de Clercq–Temperley Rock Corpus** (the one citable, CC BY 4.0, *pop/rock* transition source). Ship the tiny matrix inline; do **not** ship a dataset. Optionally allow a live Hooktheory Trends API escalation.
- **Key-fit: diatonic-membership count minus a circle-of-fifths distance penalty for non-diatonic chords, pick the best key, then disambiguate relative major/minor with first/last-chord + cadence weighting.**
- **Verdict = two independent axes:** per-chord *diatonic-fit* label (is the chord in the key?) and per-transition *plausibility* score (is the move common?). Combine, but keep them separate in the output — that's what makes it explainable and honest.

---

## 1. Roman-numeral analysis + key detection — library vs hand-roll

### What `music21` actually gives you

- **Roman numerals:** `roman.romanNumeralFromChord(chordObj, keyObj=None, preferSecondaryDominants=False)` returns a `RomanNumeral` with `.scaleDegree` (int), `.quality`, `.figure` (e.g. `'bVII65/V'`), `.figureAndKey`, `.romanNumeral`. It even does secondary-dominant labelling. Docs: [music21.roman module](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleRoman.html), [User's Guide ch. 23](https://music21.org/music21docs/usersGuide/usersGuide_23_romanNumerals.html).
- **Chord-symbol parsing is a *different* class:** `roman` works on `chord.Chord` objects, not text. Text symbols like `"F#m7b5"`, `"Cadd9"`, `"G/B"` go through `harmony.ChordSymbol(...)` → returns a Chord you then feed to `romanNumeralFromChord`. Docs: [music21.harmony](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleHarmony.html).
- **Key detection:** `stream.analyze('key')` delegates to `analysis.discrete`, which ships multiple profile weightings — Krumhansl–Schmuckler / Krumhansl–Kessler, Aarden-Essen, Bellman–Budge, Temperley–Kostka–Payne, Simple. Docs: [analysis.discrete](https://music21.org/music21docs/moduleReference/moduleAnalysisDiscrete.html), [User's Guide ch. 15](https://music21.org/music21docs/usersGuide/usersGuide_15_key.html). (Confirm exact class names against `analysis.discrete` at build time — the search surfaced Krumhansl and Aarden-Essen in core but the naming is worth a one-line check.)

### Dependency weight / `uv run` behavior

- The `music21` wheel itself is **`py3-none-any` (pure Python)**, Python **&gt;=3.10**, but its **runtime deps are numpy, matplotlib, chardet, jsonpickle, requests, more-itertools, webcolors, joblib** ([piwheels metadata](https://www.piwheels.org/project/music21/), [pyproject.toml](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/blob/master/pyproject.toml), [requirements.txt](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/blob/master/requirements.txt)). numpy and matplotlib carry **compiled binary wheels** — they resolve fine under `uv run` on mainstream macOS/Linux/Windows (prebuilt wheels exist), but they're the opposite of "lean": tens of MB, non-trivial cold resolve, and matplotlib is pure dead weight for a text validator. `uv` will cache it, so it's a one-time cost, but it still bloats the script's dependency surface.

### `ChordSymbol` parsing gotchas (the reason not to lean on it)

Known open bugs bite exactly the chords a ChordPro sheet contains: [#1570 — `addb7` yields a doubly-flatted seventh; slash chords with extensions decode wrong](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/issues/1570), and [#197 — invalid behavior with `sus`/`aug`](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/issues/197). `m7b5` (half-diminished) and basic `add9` are supported via `CHORD_TYPES`, and you can extend that dict, but you'd be normalizing strings *before* handing them over anyway — at which point you've already written most of a parser.

### The hand-roll — tractable, and the fiddly parts

Very tractable for this narrow job. The pieces:

1. **Chord-symbol tokenizer** (~40–70 lines): regex `root (A–G, #/b) | quality suffix | /bass`. Root+bass → pitch-class 0–11. Quality → a small set (maj, min, dim, aug, dom7, maj7, min7, m7b5, sus2/4, add9, 6…). You only need *quality* to a resolution that affects the Roman-numeral case (upper vs lower) and any °/ø/+ decoration.
2. **Diatonic-triad tables** (two 7-row tables):
   - Major: **I ii iii IV V vi vii°** (maj, min, min, maj, maj, min, dim).
   - Minor: **i ii° III iv v/V VI VII/vii°** — natural minor is `i ii° III iv v VI VII`; harmonic-minor practice raises 7 so `v→V` and `VII→vii°`. Handle both variants.
3. **Roman/Nashville emitter**: degree number relative to the key's tonic, cased by quality, prefixed with accidental for non-diatonic roots (`bVII`, `#iv`), figured-bass suffix for inversions from the `/bass` (`6`, `6/4`).

The genuinely fiddly bits — flag these in the reference doc:

- **Enharmonic spelling is not `pc % 12`.** You must spell each root by *letter name relative to the key's scale*, or you'll mislabel `bVII` vs `#VI`, or call IV in F-major (`Bb`) a `#III`. Build a per-key letter-spelled scale (key-signature aware), then compute the degree by letter distance, and derive the accidental from the actual vs. diatonic pitch. This is the single most error-prone part and the main thing `music21` gets right for free.
- **Minor-key harmonic/natural variants:** decide whether to report `v` or `V`, `bVII` or `vii°`, and whether a raised-6/7 chord is diatonic-in-context. Simplest honest rule: treat *both* natural and harmonic/melodic diatonic sets as "in key," and label the mode variant.
- **Borrowed / secondary chords:** you can cheaply label a fixed common set — mixture chords `bVII bIII bVI iv`, Neapolitan `bII`, and secondary dominants (a major/dom7 chord whose root is a fifth above a diatonic degree → `V/x`). Full, reliable secondary-dominant/augmented-sixth analysis is where you'd escalate to `music21`.
- **Slash chords:** map `/bass` to inversion figured bass when the bass is a chord tone, else note it as a pedal/added bass (`IV/1` style) rather than forcing a wrong inversion.

### Recommendation for section 1

**Hand-roll the core (zero deps), escalate to `music21` optionally.** The parse-and-label job is small, and hand-rolling keeps the output *explainable* (you emit the exact Roman/Nashville strings the user thinks in) and dodges the `ChordSymbol` bugs. Reserve `music21` — behind a PEP 723 `[project.optional-dependencies]`/`--with` flag or a `try: import` — for two things it does markedly better: **profile-based key detection** (Krumhansl/Aarden) as a cross-check, and **secondary-dominant / chromatic analysis** when the hand-roll labels something "out-of-key" that's really a `V/V`.

Network + auth dependency, not shippable offline. | Proprietary; API-gated |
| **CoCoPops / Billboard** ([repo](https://github.com/Computational-Cognitive-Musicology-Lab/CoCoPops)) | Humdrum re-encoding of McGill Billboard | Alt encoding if you prefer Humdrum tooling | — |
| **Chordonomicon** ([arXiv 2410.22046](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.22046)) | 666k songs' chord progressions | Overkill to ship; cite as "big-data corroboration" | — |
| **UMass "Fundamentals of Music Theory," Unit 18** ([page](https://fundamentalsofmusictheory.umasscreate.net/unit-18/)) | Reproduces a pop/rock two-chord succession table (from the rock corpus) side-by-side with a classical one | Handy secondary citation; source of the concrete `V→IV = 28%` (pop) vs `7%` (classical) datapoint | — |

**Key empirical facts to bake into the prior and the caveats** (from de Clercq–Temperley / UMass): rock is **less goal-directed** than classical; **IV** is the most common non-tonic and **plagal IV→I** is pervasive; **`bVII→IV→I`** ("double-plagal") is a signature rock move; **`V→IV`** (a classical "retrogression") happens ~**28%** of the time in pop vs ~**7%** classical. The load-bearing consequence: **a classical-syntax transition prior will over-flag legitimate rock progressions.** Use a rock-derived prior, and say so.

### The functional-harmony theory prior (the defensible hand-authored option)

Yes — a small hand-authored first-order matrix over Roman-numeral *functions* is a standard, defensible approach for *validation* (as opposed to generation). Map degrees to functions — **T** = I, vi, (iii); **PD/S** = IV, ii; **D** = V, vii° — and encode the canonical tendencies: **V→I strong, ii→V→I, IV→I (plagal), IV→V, vi→IV, V→vi (deceptive), I→anything**, with low weight on true retrogressions (but *not* zero, per the rock data). References for the function mapping and tendencies: [Open Music Theory — Harmonic Functions](https://openmusictheory.github.io/harmonicFunctions.html), [Wikipedia — I–V–vi–IV progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I%E2%80%93V%E2%80%93vi%E2%80%93IV_progression). Markov-over-chords is a well-trodden method (e.g. the ["Write Like Taylor Swift" first-order chord Markov chain](https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/113839_da12af8738fb4774a22bd62f35666287.html)).

### Recommendation for section 2

Ship a **hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral transition matrix (~7×7 diatonic + a few common chromatic rows like `bVII`, `V/V`), with the numbers anchored to the de Clercq–Temperley rock corpus**, not to classical theory. This is the simplest *defensible, citable, offline* model. Score a progression as the mean (or geometric mean) log-probability of its steps; flag any step below a percentile/threshold as "suspect." Offer the **Hooktheory `/trends/nodes` API as an optional live cross-check** for users who want empirical current-DB probabilities.

**Combining the two axes into a readable verdict** — keep them orthogonal:

- **Diatonic-fit** flags the *chord* (in-key / borrowed / secondary / out-of-key).
- **Transition-probability** flags the *move* (this step is rare).
- A chord can be diatonic yet a rare move, or non-diatonic yet an extremely common move (`bVII`, `V/V`). So the strongest "**likely mis-transcribed**" signal is **the conjunction**: a low-probability transition *into* a chord that's also out-of-key. A rare move into a diatonic chord is "unusual but plausible"; a borrowed chord reached by a common move is "colorful, fine." Present per-chord labels and per-transition scores separately, then a combined verdict.

---

## 3. Circle of fifths for key-fit / detection

**Scoring recipe (simple, explainable):** for each of the 24 candidate keys, `score(K) = (# chords diatonic in K) − λ · Σ(circle-of-fifths distance of each non-diatonic chord root from K's tonic)`. Pick the argmax. Circle-of-fifths distance encodes relatedness: a chord one step around the circle (e.g. the V's own dominant, or `bVII`) is "near" and cheap; a tritone away is "far" and expensive. This is a lightweight, deterministic stand-in for the Krumhansl–Schmuckler profile correlation, and it's fully auditable (you can print the per-key tally). Background: [rnhart.net — key-finding / Krumhansl–Schmuckler](https://rnhart.net/articles/key-finding/), [Temperley 1999 KS re-evaluation](https://davidtemperley.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/temperley-mp99.pdf), [interactive circle of fifths + diatonic sets](https://www.guitarcomposerstoolbox.com/circle-of-fifths/). If you want a probabilistically-grounded variant, weight chord roots by a key profile instead of a flat diatonic count — that's exactly what `music21`'s Krumhansl/Aarden classes do, and is the natural escalation.

**The relative-major/minor pitfall (C vs Am):** they share an identical diatonic set, so *diatonic membership alone cannot tell them apart* — this is the canonical key-detection failure, which [MIREX Audio Key Detection](https://www.music-ir.org/mirex/wiki/2026%3AAudio_Key_Detection) even codifies by giving *partial credit* for relative/parallel/fifth errors. Disambiguate with **tonic-emphasis cues, not the pitch-class set**:

- **First and (especially) last chord** — progressions tend to start and end on the tonic. The final chord is the strongest single cue.
- **Cadence weighting** — a `V→I` at a phrase end nails major; `V→i` (or `bVII→i`, `iv→i`) nails minor. (This is precisely the fix the practitioner literature recommends for tools that mis-call minor: [goatwaveaudio — fixing AI key detection](https://goatwaveaudio.com/blog/fixing-ai-key-detection/).)
- **Bass / duration emphasis** — total time or count the presumed tonic chord dominates.
- If it's genuinely ambiguous, **report both and say so** (honest &gt; confident-wrong), consistent with the skill's existing "Detected key is a suggestion" gotcha.

---

## Concrete recommended design (put this in `references/music-theory.md`)

**Dependency choice:** zero-dep hand-rolled core in a PEP 723 `uv run` script; `music21` behind an optional extra / `try-import` for (a) Krumhansl/Aarden key cross-check and (b) secondary-dominant analysis. Matches the skill's existing self-contained-script convention.

**Pipeline:** ChordPro `[..]` extraction → chord-symbol parse (root+quality+bass) → candidate-key scoring (diatonic count − λ·circle-distance) → relative-major/minor disambiguation (first/last chord + cadence) → Roman-numeral + Nashville emission in the chosen key → per-chord diatonic-fit labels → first-order transition scoring against the rock-corpus-seeded matrix → verdict.

**Transition model:** inline hand-authored first-order Roman-numeral matrix, numbers anchored to de Clercq–Temperley (CC BY 4.0, attribute it); optional Hooktheory `/trends/nodes` live cross-check.

**Output verdict — what it should look like:**

- **Detected key** + confidence, with the runner-up named when relative/parallel is close ("G major, or possibly E minor — final chord is G, so G major").
- **Per-chord table:** `chord | Roman | Nashville | label` where label ∈ {diatonic, borrowed (bVII…), secondary (V/V…), out-of-key}.
- **Per-transition flags:** the low-probability steps, each shown as `Xrare→ Y (p≈…, expected: …)`, framed as **"review — surprising but maybe intentional,"** *not* "wrong."
- **Overall plausibility score** (0–1 or a letter), = combination of diatonic-fit ratio and mean transition log-prob.
- **Suspect list** = the conjunction cases (out-of-key chord reached by a rare move) → *"likely mis-transcribed; double-check."*
- **Honesty footer:** the prior is rock-derived and descriptive, not prescriptive; unusual ≠ wrong; key may be ambiguous.

**Honest caveats to surface in the doc:** (1) a first-order Markov prior can't see the actual voice-leading or a modulation, so it flags surprising-but-valid moves — hence "review," not "error"; (2) rock legitimately breaks classical rules (`V→IV`, `bVII→IV→I`), so a classical prior over-flags — use the rock prior; (3) relative-major/minor is fundamentally ambiguous from the chord set alone; (4) enharmonic spelling depends on the chosen key, so a wrong key detection cascades into wrong Roman numerals.

## Context

The `chordpro` skill already ships (author→eval→improve, 3 iterations). But charting
~10 C-pop songs surfaced two quality problems the user named directly: the
**chord-change timing vs. the lyrics** and the **overall chord progression** aren't
captured well.

Inspecting two real outputs pinpoints the cause — and it's an instruction written
*into* the skill, not a one-off slip:

- `~/Documents/chord-sheets/jay-chou-shuohao-buku/shuohao-buku.cho`, chorus:
  `眼看[G]著妳[B7]難過[Em7] [G/D] 挽[Cmaj7]留…沒有說[G] [D7]` — the `[G/D]`, `[G]`, `[D7]`
  are **floating** (sit over no syllable).
- `~/Documents/chord-sheets/li-ronghao-libai/li-ronghao-libai.cho`, verse 1:
  `[F]大部分人要我[F]學習… 世俗的[C]眼光[C]` — a **duplicate** `[F]…[F]` and a trailing `[C]`.

Root cause: `references/chord-tab-sources.md` steps 3–4 tell the agent to fetch
lyrics *separately* from LRCLIB, treat those as ground truth, and **re-align the
chart's chords onto them by eyeball** — discarding the one piece of ground-truth
alignment the chart already had (Chord4's `你不是真正(的)快樂` markup encodes exactly
which syllable each chord lands on). Floaters and duplicates are what fall out of a
lossy re-merge.

**Outcome of this change:** (1) preserve the source chart's own alignment via a
deterministic parser so the drift class disappears at the source; (2) add a
music-theory validator that detects the key, expresses every chord as a scale

# Rock chord-transition data — de Clercq & Temperley (2011)

## Good news: the full matrix IS published

Your worry that the paper "may only give aggregate successions" is unfounded. **Table 3 of the paper is a complete 12×12 transition matrix** over all Roman-numeral roots, given as **raw co-occurrence counts** (antecedent → consequent). I extracted it verbatim from the PDF you linked. Everything below is directly sourced; the only thing I computed is row-normalization (simple division of the sourced counts), which I mark clearly.

Source for Tables 2–4: de Clercq & Temperley 2011, pp. 60–62, PDF at `https://davidtemperley.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/declercq-temperley-pm11.pdf`

---

## CRITICAL: how the paper labels chords (read this before coding)

The paper uses **root categories only** — capital Roman numerals denote a *scale-degree root*, with **chord quality (major/minor/dim) deliberately collapsed**, and **applied chords folded in**. So in this dataset:

- `II`  = **both** diatonic `ii` **and** `II`(=V/V) — one merged category
- `III` = **both** `iii` **and** `III`(=V/vi)
- `VI`  = **both** `vi` **and** `VI`(=V/ii)
- `VII` = the diatonic **leading-tone root** `vii°` (raised 7th) — distinct from `bVII`
- `I`, `IV`, `V` as expected; `bII, bIII, #IV, bVI, bVII` are the chromatic roots

This means the "diatonic ii vs V/V" distinction you asked me to separate **does not exist in the source** — they are the same cell. Do not double-list them. If your validator needs quality (`ii` minor vs `II` major), that information is *not* recoverable from this table; you'd layer it separately.

Direction convention in Table 3: **rows = antecedent (current chord), columns = consequent (next chord).** Reading across a row gives you "what follows X" (i.e. P(next | current)). Reading down a column gives "what precedes X" (the pre-tonic view the paper discusses).

---

### Your anchor datapoint, reconciled
- **Paper's own numbers:** V→IV raw = **392**, normalized **392/1488 = 0.263** (or 392/1516 total-V = 0.259). So ≈ **26%**.

So the classical-vs-rock V→IV contrast (7% vs ~26–28%) holds; treat 26% as the citable value and 28% as a secondary rounding. ## Filling zero cells (only if you need a generative model)

The full matrix is published, so **nothing needs inventing.** But many cells are hard 0 due to sparsity (only 99 songs). If you want nonzero probabilities everywhere, do **not** fabricate numbers — apply principled smoothing:

- **Additive (add-k) with the marginal as prior:** `P(next|cur) = (count[cur][next] + α·marginal[next]) / (rowtotal[cur] + α)`, using `ROOT_MARGINAL` proportions as `marginal[next]` and small `α` (e.g. 1–5). This backs off rare rows (bII, #IV, VII — row totals 45/17/37) toward the overall root distribution, which is exactly the functional-harmony-agnostic "preference hierarchy" the authors argue rock actually follows (they note rock's pre-tonic, post-tonic, and overall distributions all rank IV > V > bVII, i.e. context matters less than in classical). Mark any smoothed cell as INTERPOLATED in your code.

---

## Minor-key handling

The corpus is **tonic-relative and mode-agnostic at the root level**: every song is centered on its own tonic = `I`, capital numerals default to major-scale degrees, and Aeolian/minor songs are represented through the **flat-side roots** `bIII, bVI, bVII` (and minor `i`, which shares the `I` cell). Roughly a third of the corpus is modal/minor, and those songs are *already baked into this single matrix.*

**Recommendation — Option A (keep the song's own tonic as `I`; use this one matrix as-is).** A minor-key Aeolian vamp like Am–G–F–G is analyzed by the authors as `I–bVII–bVI–bVII`, which is fully represented (I→bVII=0.159, bVII→bVI=0.155, bVI→bVII=0.213). This matches how the data was actually built, so the statistics stay valid. No separate minor matrix is needed or published.

Avoid **Option B (remap minor `i` to relative-major `vi`)**: it re-centers the tonal frame away from the actual tonic, which contradicts the corpus construction and distorts the numbers. Only consider it if your validator is hard-wired to major-mode function labels and cannot treat `I` as a possibly-minor tonic.

Caveat either way: because quality is collapsed, this matrix **cannot tell you** whether the tonic is major or minor — that's a separate detection layer.
